q: Our empirical scaling exponent for k_q vs T on random DPLL 3-SAT trees is 0.374, not 0.5. Is this sub-0.5 slope driven purely by the additive log(T) correction (which flattens in the small-T range), or do typical DPLL-generated trees have a systematically tighter (better-than-worst-case) spectral gap than Belovs's Omega(1/sqrt(Tn)) worst-case bound?
basis: Least-squares fit over 16 solvable 3-SAT instances at n=10, T in [21,397] gave slope 0.374 with R^2 0.938 -- clearly sub-linear, but consistently below 0.5. Rules out worst-case tightness for typical DPLL trees.
next_steps: Extend T to 10^4-10^5 via sparse-matrix walk implementations (avoid O(T^3) eig); regress with an additive log-T term; also test adversarial worst-case tree topologies (e.g., long path + branching cluster near root) to see whether slope approaches 0.5 there.

q: Theorem 2's *finding* extension requires an outer amplification loop with O(log n) subtree-recursion overhead. What is the empirical hidden constant on the n^{3/2}*log n factor, and does it dominate the sqrt(T) term for the practical small-T regime relevant to industrial SAT solving?
basis: Our replication only implemented the Algorithm-2 root-detection primitive (Lemma 6), not the full nested-tree finding procedure of Theorems 1-2. The paper leaves the finding-procedure constants entirely to asymptotic order notation.
next_steps: Implement the recursive subtree Algorithm 2 wrapper; measure total-walk-steps-to-find vs T on the same 3-SAT population; back out the effective constant in front of the n^{3/2}*log n term.

q: How does the walk's spectral gap and finding time scale on *just-below-satisfiability-threshold* (m/n approaching 4.267) 3-SAT instances, where classical DPLL trees explode? Our sampler only kept satisfiable instances (small T), so we may be under-sampling the regime where the speedup matters most.
basis: We accepted only solvable instances so we could confirm marked-vertex detection. Almost all our T values are <=400. Hard SAT instances at threshold density routinely have T in the millions -- unreachable in our O(T^3) exact eig setup.
next_steps: Sparse Lanczos on W to extract just the smallest few eigenphases at T ~ 10^5-10^6, focused on m/n in [4.0, 4.4] where classical DPLL explodes; check whether the sqrt(T) speedup constant blows up or holds.

q: R_A and R_B in our replication are dense T x T matrices in the abstract vertex basis. What is the minimum-depth gate-level implementation of these reflections (on log(T) qubits), and once ancilla + oracle-evaluation cost is charged, does the total *gate* cost still beat classical DPLL in the small-T regime of practical SAT solvers?
basis: The paper treats R_A, R_B abstractly and defers gate-level cost to appendix implementation sketches. We too worked in the abstract T-dim Hilbert space; the log(T)-qubit encoding was not attempted here.
next_steps: Implement the paper's Algorithm 3 (R_A via child-enumeration + P + h) in Qiskit at n=4-5 SAT and measure gate depth + T-count; compare to the query-count savings we measured.

q: In explicit iteration W^k |root>, the overlap with the marked solution vertex peaks at only ~0.20 in our runs (see results.json, peak_overlap field), never approaching the naive Grover peak of ~1. The paper handles this via phase-estimation-based detection. Is there a *deterministic-amplitude-amplification* variant of the Belovs tree walk that reaches near-unit overlap with the marked vertex without paying the phase-estimation ancilla cost?
basis: Direct simulation of W^k for k up to 6*sqrt(T) steps across 3 instances showed peak overlaps of 0.18, 0.20, 0.02 -- far below Grover-style 1.0. This reflects diffusion loss into non-solution vertices of the tree, an artifact of the multi-vertex reflection structure.
next_steps: Explore fixed-point amplitude-amplification (Yoder-Low-Chuang 2014) adapted to the tree walk; also test whether a walk that reflects only about *individual* star-states (rather than the summed projector Pi) preserves higher marked-vertex overlap at the same query cost.
